strengths: The paper identifies a useful problem for black-box auditing: interpretable macro-level features can be confounded with predictions even when the raw model inputs are not. This perspective has an identifiable audience in explainability and causal discovery.

PAG learning is a principled framework for representing latent confounding and causal ambiguity under the stated assumptions. The background knowledge that predictions cannot cause image content is well motivated.

The structural causal model, graphical examples, and distinction between population-level and individual explanations communicate the central proposal clearly. The discussion acknowledges important limitations involving faithfulness, measurement error, feature construction, and incomplete identification.

The omitted-feature simulation provides a concrete illustration, while the two image applications, bootstrap analyses, and alternative discovery algorithm make the proposal more tangible. Applying established methods to this problem is a worthwhile contribution without requiring a new algorithm.
weaknesses: Necessary: Several empirical conclusions exceed what the reported graph summaries establish. Section 6.3 pools directed and partially directed edges, although a consistently partially directed edge can remain compatible with pure confounding. Moreover, a missing adjacency does not imply absence of a causal effect: a feature can affect predictions through another observed feature. The negative causal statements in Figures 9–10 and Section 6.4 therefore require correction. Report definite and possible ancestry using the full graphs, distinguish endpoint types, and avoid interpreting bootstrap stability as a probability of causation.

Necessary: The X-ray sampling design needs a selection-bias analysis. Section 6.1 selects 120 pneumonia images and 120 controls with 'no findings,' so inclusion depends on disease status and the explanatory findings. This can change the conditional-independence structure, whereas Section 3 dismisses selection bias as irrelevant. Allowing latent confounding does not by itself justify the paper's causal interpretation under this sampling scheme. Account for selection, justify an appropriate alternative sampling design, or explicitly limit this application to an exploratory illustration.

Necessary: Example 1 and Appendix A need a consistent definition of the Shapley coalition value. Appendix A.1 evaluates interventions on Z2 and Z3 while leaving Z1 at its observational distribution, although both variables cause Z1 in the stated SCM. Those calculations describe replacement of prediction-function arguments rather than the corresponding macro-variable interventions. Appendix A.2 also retains the unobserved z3 in the purported calculation with that feature omitted. Define the intervention target and available information, then correct the comparison. A zero attribution for one instance also does not establish absence of population-level causal relevance.

Necessary: The real-data evidence does not adequately establish the reliability of the reported feature conclusions. Chi-square conditional-independence tests face potentially sparse tables with 240 X-rays and with 26 multivalued bird attributes and conditioning sets up to size four; relevant count diagnostics and sparse-table handling are not reported. Bootstrapping does not resolve systematic testing errors. Additionally, Appendix C substantially changes the bird ranking, placing Crown Color and Size highest instead of the leading FCI features. Clarify the graph-learning sample, assess test reliability, and make the substantive conclusions reflect this sensitivity; otherwise narrow the empirical claims.

Optional: Repeated synthetic experiments with controlled shape interventions would quantify recovery reliability beyond the single illustration. Comparisons using the same macro-level annotations would also help separate the benefit of causal discovery from the benefit of supplying interpretable features, which the pixel-level LIME/SHAP comparisons do not isolate.
